title: Rugby league
description: Full-contact sport played by two teams of thirteen players on a rectangular field
wiki_lead:
Rugby league football, commonly known as rugby league, is a full-contact sport played by two teams of thirteen players on a rectangular field measuring 68 m (74 yd) wide and 112–122 m (122–133 yd) long with H-shaped posts at both ends. It is one of the two major codes of rugby football, the other being rugby union. 
It originated in 1895 in Huddersfield,  West Yorkshire, and England, as the result of a split from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) over the issue of payments to players. The rules of the game governed by the new Northern Rugby Football Union progressively changed from those of the RFU with the specific aim of producing a faster and more entertaining game to appeal to paying spectators, on whose income the new organisation and its members depended.
In rugby league, points are scored by carrying an oval ball and touching it to the ground beyond the opposing team's goal line; this is called a try, and is the primary method of scoring, worth four points. The opposing team attempts to stop the attacking side scoring points by tackling the player carrying the ball and denying forward progress. On occasion, where a clear try scoring opportunity has been thwarted by foul play, a penalty try may be awarded without the ball being grounded over the try line. In addition to tries, points can be scored by kicking goals. Drop goals (or field goals) can be attempted from the hand at any time for a single point. Following a successful try, the scoring team gains a free kick to try at goal with a conversion worth a further two points. Penalty kicks at goal, known simply as penalties, may also be awarded for general foul play, and are also worth two points. Unlike drop goals, penalty kicks and conversions are taken from the ground, with the ball usually set in a kicking tee, and the opposing team not allowed to directly challenge the kicker.
The National Rugby League (NRL) in Australia/New Zealand and the Super League in Europe are the world's premier club competitions. Rugby league is played internationally, predominantly by Australasian, European, and Pacific Island countries, and is governed by the International Rugby League. Rugby league is the national sport of Papua New Guinea and the Cook Islands and is a popular sport in countries such as England, Australia, New Zealand, Tonga, Fiji and Samoa.
The first Rugby League World Cup was held in France in 1954, the first World Cup of either rugby code, and has been held sporadically ever since, settling into a four-yearly cycle in the 2010s; as of 2023, the holders are Australia.
The first Women's Rugby League World Cup was held in 2000 and New Zealand won the inaugural title. The holders are Australia.
A short-sided version of the sport, rugby league nines, using modified rugby league rules also exists, and is comparable to rugby sevens. Wheelchair rugby league is a mixed-gender sport using heavily modified rugby league rules for disabled and able-bodied players. Unlike wheelchair rugby which adopted its name after the invention of the sport previously called murderball and is not directly linked to rugby union, wheelchair rugby league has grown out of the parent sport, and retains key aspects of that sport such as an egg shaped ball, the forward-pass rule and conversions. While not a Paralympic sport, the sport has its own Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup. A further variation for ambulatory disabled players, physical disability rugby league, was created and had its first world cup in 2022 to coincide with the rescheduled 2021 Rugby League World Cup competitions.

Etymology
Rugby league football takes its name from the bodies that split to create a new form of rugby, distinct from that run by the Rugby Football Unions, in Britain, Australia, and New Zealand between 1895 and 1908. grok_lead: Rugby league is a full-contact team sport played between two teams of 13 players on a rectangular field approximately 100 meters long, with the objective of scoring points by grounding the oval ball in the opponent's in-goal area to achieve a try worth four points or by successful kicks at goal. The sport emerged in 1895 from a schism in northern England, where 22 clubs from industrial areas formed the Northern Rugby Football Union to compensate working-class players for lost wages, rejecting the Rugby Football Union's strict amateurism that favored southern, wealthier participants. This breakaway prioritized professionalism and modified rules to suit faster, more open play, distinguishing it from rugby union through elements like six tackles per possession rather than continuous contests for the ball. Governed internationally by the International Rugby League since 2016, the sport organizes events like the Rugby League World Cup, first held in 1954, and maintains world rankings led by Australia, New Zealand, and England. Its core rules, outlined in the official Laws of the Game, emphasize tackling below the shoulders, quick play-the-balls after each tackle, and unlimited interchange substitutions to sustain high intensity, with matches lasting 80 minutes divided into two halves. Professional leagues dominate, including Australia's National Rugby League (NRL), featuring 17 teams and drawing millions of viewers annually, and England's Super League, contested by 12 clubs primarily in the north. Rugby league's popularity centers on Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, northern England, and France, where it serves as a cultural staple among working-class communities, though global expansion faces challenges from rugby union's Olympic status and broader institutional support. Defining characteristics include its causal emphasis on territorial advancement via short kicks and powerful runs, fostering rivalries like Australia's State of Origin series, which attracts over 90,000 spectators per match. Early controversies revolved around the 1895 split's class tensions, with northern clubs viewing RFU policies as elitist barriers to fair compensation, a realism that propelled rugby league's resilience despite limited media amplification compared to union.
